Source: http://www.thestar.com/

Posted May 10, 2000
(MarijuanaNews note: This item happens to be about a Canadian survey, but it is very similar in every way to the sort of thing that happens in DEAland and elsewhere. No coincidence. Prohibitionism is an international ideology.

This article is also characteristic of the " civic duty " reporting that treats almost anything labeled " anti-drug " as a " good thing. " The reporter is just covering his beat and seems to know nothing about the subject, but critical thinking on " drugs " is not encouraged for journalists or other impressionable minds.

One of the great advantages we have over the prohibitionists is that not only do they seem clueless as to what we are actually saying, they seem to be incapable of understanding their own data.

This short piece offers an insight into why marijuana prohibition is not just a failure, but actually counterproductive. It muddles the meaning of words, and despairs that students have accurate views on some things, and politically incorrect views on others. It also fails to comprehend that what they are documenting it that marijuana prohibition is a fiasco.

None of that matters. The real concern seems to be maintaining marijuana prohibition. That is apparent in most such stories.)

By Bob Mitchell, Peel/Halton Bureau Chief

FEWER STUDENTS SEE RISK IN DRUGS
Narcotics Easy To Get, Study Finds
(MarijuanaNews note: As we will see, the word " narcotics " is used as a synonym for " drugs. " Of course, " drugs " means " marijuana " -- except when it doesn't.)
See
" Mom, Dad, What are Drugs? "

An alarming number of Halton students think there is no harm in taking drugs, a new study says.
(MarijuanaNews note: Actually, that is not what the story says at all. It is about perceieved risk in single usage. That is not the same thing as thinking that " there is no harm in taking drugs. " )

And students say narcotics such as cocaine and LSD are easy to obtain.
(MarijuanaNews note: Of course, LSD is not a " narcotic, " but a hallucinogen. Cocaine is a stimulant, the opposite of a " narcotic. " Marijuana is none of the above.)

" About 18 per cent of the students basically felt it was easy or very easy to access cocaine, and almost 23 per cent said they could easily obtain LSD, " said Dr. Robert Nosal, Halton's medical officer of health. " And 51.2 per cent said marijuana was very easy to obtain. "
(MarijuanaNews note: Well, at least marijuana is easier to get than cocaine, but this does not say much about the success of prohibition.)

The study released Friday surveyed 3,304 students in Grades 7 and 8 and high school in Oakville, Burlington, Halton Hills and Milton between February and April, 1999.

According to the survey, only 29 per cent of the students said they felt there was any " great risk " associated with trying cocaine once or twice, compared to almost 43 per cent who said it was risky in a 1991 Ontario-wide drug survey.
(MarijuanaNews note: Well, how much risk is there in trying cocaine once or twice. While there have probably been some deaths from single doses of cocaine, they are very rare, so the risk is very low for a single dose. Why is it considered alarming for students to have an accurate opinion?)

While police are seeing an incredible increase in the use of ecstasy in the club scene and on the street, powdered cocaine and its offshoot, crack cocaine, remain their biggest concern.

The survey also suggested surging acceptance of marijuana among local students. Forty-three per cent of the Halton students said they strongly disapproved of adults using marijuana.
(MarijuanaNews note: Why is a question about approval of " adults using marijuana " relevant in a survey supposedly concerned about students’ use?

After all, adults do lots of things that children are not supposed to do. Notice the emphasis on this number in the next sentence. In fact, this would appear to be tracking the status of support for marijuana prohibition, not marijuana use by children.)
See
Campus Magazine Survey Says Only 36% Of College Students " feel that marijuana should remain illegal. " But they downplay the results.

While that's the same figure a provincewide teen survey reached last year, it's a drop of 18 points from the 61 per cent of Ontario teens who disapproved in a 1991 survey.

Almost as many students said they had tried marijuana (26 per cent) as had smoked a cigarette (28 per cent), and almost 40 per cent of marijuana users said they smoked at least 10 joints in the past year.
(MarijuanaNews note: That is less than once per month. The risk of using marijuana at that level would have to be extremely low, even for the younger students.)

To nobody's surprise, however, alcohol was the drug of choice for the majority of Halton students - and its use is increasing, Nosal said.
(MarijuanaNews note: Where are the numbers? The data on the student’s attitudes toward adult marijuana use is given, but not on their use of alcohol.)
